page.after:
What the differences mean

  • WTA09 against WTA07: the WTA09 costs $15.00 less ($42.99 − $27.99), has a second AC outlet and the same 65 W USB-C3 port. In exchange it weighs 1.14 oz more (7.18 − 6.04 oz).
  • Cost per laptop watt: WTA09 $0.43/W ($27.99 ÷ 65), Ceptics $0.57/W ($39.99 ÷ 70), WTA07 $0.66/W ($42.99 ÷ 65), TA-105 Pro $0.71/W ($49.99 ÷ 70), Pulse Duo $0.77/W ($49.99 ÷ 65).
  • The 70 W headroom: 70 − 65 = 5 W more, and only through a 5 A cable. Through a 3 A cable the 65 W and 70 W adapters all stop at 20 V × 3 A = 60 W.
  • What a plain cable costs you: on a 65 W port, 5 W of 65 (7.7%). On a 70 W port, 10 W of 70 (14%). If your laptop's own charger is rated 60 W or less, a 3 A cable costs you nothing.
  • EPICKA Air 65W: TrekSavvy, quoting EPICKA's manual, says the 65 W port drops to 40 W plus 15 W once a second USB port is in use. That leaves the laptop 40 ÷ 65 = 62% of its headline power. Laurence Norah of Finding the Universe weighed it at 149 g, lighter than either TESSAN (the WTA07's 6.04 oz is 171 g).

Why the cable decides whether you actually get 65W

A USB-C laptop charges at 20 V, and watts are volts times amps. 65 W at 20 V needs 3.25 A, and 70 W needs 3.5 A. A USB-C cable without an e-marker chip is limited to 3 A. Anker's support page says it directly: "To achieve output over 60W, an E-Marker cable must be used; without it, only 3A current is supported." Satechi says the same from the cable side: once a charger puts out more than 3 A, "a 5A wire with an E-Mark chip will be required." So every adapter in the table stops at 60 W on an ordinary 3 A cable, however it is labelled.

The fix costs less than a meal. Pack a cable rated 100 W or more: 100 W at 20 V is 5 A. Baseus's 100 W USB-C cable is listed at $9.99 on Baseus's store (2026-11-13) {buy:baseus-usb-c-cable-100w}. Baseus's 240 W cable ($12.99, same store and date) says on its listing that it has an E-marker chip. If the cable you already own is printed 60 W or 3 A, that is where your laptop will stop.

Port choice matters as much as the cable. On both TESSANs, only USB-C3 reaches 65 W. TESSAN rates the other four ports at 15 W max each, and it states the 65 W for single-port use.

Not recommended

Paying extra for the EPICKA TA-105 Pro's 70 W. At $49.99 it costs $22.00 more than the WTA09 ($49.99 − $27.99) for 5 W more. Those 5 W need a 5 A cable, which you also need to get the WTA09's full 65 W. On a 3 A cable both deliver 60 W. EPICKA's listing doesn't say how much the 70 W port keeps when the other ports are busy.
